query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear performance of high-entropy alloy protective coatings is primarily governed by a dynamic mechanism in which an optimally refined grain structure promotes the formation of a robust, crack‐resistant oxide glaze during sliding. This glaze acts as a self-healing, low-shear barrier that mitigates adhesive and oxidative wear, while coarser grain structures yield unstable oxide films that crack under repeated stress.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA coatings (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi or similar compositions) in a state with a baseline, coarser grain size distribution and oxide‐free surfaces.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal or mechanical treatment to refine the grain size (i.e., produce a fine-grained microstructure) prior to wear testing.
generation.conditions: Perform sliding wear tests under atmospheric conditions across a range of normal loads and sliding speeds at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures where frictional heating induces oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The grain boundaries and the microstructure of the developing oxide glaze layer at the friction interface.
generation.mechanism: Finer grains increase the surface hardness and enhance the adhesion and continuity of a friction-induced oxide glaze. This stable oxide layer reduces the effective shear strength at the interface and resists crack formation during sliding, thereby suppressing adhesive and oxidative wear. In contrast, coatings with coarser grains form oxide layers that are prone to fracturing under high frictional stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings with refined (nanoscale or ultra-fine) grains should exhibit lower friction coefficients and specific wear rates, along with more continuous and adherent oxide layers, compared to coatings with coarser grains under similar wear conditions.
generation.baseline: HEA coatings with a coarser grain structure that develop less stable, cracked oxide films and consequently demonstrate higher friction and wear rates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for high-entropy alloy coatings similar to CoCrFeMnNi and related compositions in environments where oxidation is active (e.g., ambient air with moderate to high sliding speeds and loads). In ultra-high vacuum conditions, where oxidation is suppressed, the role of a protective oxide glaze may not be dominant.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends findings from studies on grain size effects on wear and oxide layer stability (e.g., PMC9960858) and dynamic grain-refinement with inverse Hall-Petch behavior (e.g., PMC7311485). However, the precise quantitative relationship between grain size, oxide formation kinetics, and the resultant wear performance in varying HEA compositions remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA coatings differing primarily in grain size—one with an intentionally refined, fine-grained structure and one with a coarser structure. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests under atmospheric conditions (with controlled normal loads and sliding speeds) to allow oxide glaze formation. Use high-resolution microscopy to compare the oxide layer continuity and cracking, and measure friction coefficients and specific wear rates.
measurements: Grain size distribution before and after wear
Morphology and continuity of the oxide glaze layer (via SEM/TEM)
Specific wear rate (material loss per unit load and sliding distance)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fine-grained coatings do not show statistically significant improvements in oxide glaze stability, lower friction coefficients, and reduced wear rates compared to the coarse-grained coatings, or if altering the grain size does not correlate with differences in oxide layer behavior and wear performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism
